# Caching.ai — full reference for LLMs

Caching.ai (https://caching.ai) is a drop-in caching-optimization proxy for LLM APIs, built and operated by AI3 Inc. This file is the expanded companion to https://caching.ai/llms.txt.

## The problem it solves

Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and Grok all serve repeated prompt prefixes from cache at a fraction of list price (cached input tokens typically cost ~10% of fresh ones). But the discount only applies when the cache is actually hit, and in real traffic it silently fails far more than teams expect:

- Provider prefix caches expire after roughly 5 idle minutes. One short gap between requests and the next call pays full price again.
- A single changed character at the start of a prompt (a timestamp, a request ID, a reordered tool list) silently breaks the prefix match — every call after it pays 10x.
- On Anthropic, caching is opt-in per request via cache_control breakpoints; SDK defaults don't set them.
- On the GPT-5.6 generation, plain SDK traffic stopped getting cross-request prefix caching (0% hits measured); an explicit cache breakpoint and a stable prompt_cache_key are required to restore it.
- 30–60% of a typical LLM bill is recoverable just by keeping the cache healthy — with no model or code changes.

## What the proxy does

Integration is one base-URL swap (e.g. set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to https://proxy.caching.ai and use a Caching.ai key). Your code, SDKs and request shapes stay the same. Streams pass through byte-for-byte with usage read on the fly — no buffering; analytics writes happen after the response is already on its way.

1. Cache Analytics — real hit rate, dollars saved, and dollars wasted on prompts that should have been cached, updated in real time per key and per model.
2. Cache Guard — automatic cache_control injection on Anthropic where breakpoints are missing, plus cache-breaker detection with likely-cause diagnostics (e.g. "timestamp in system prompt").
3. Cache Warmer — sends tiny low-cost pings to keep a prefix warm through idle gaps, exactly as long as it is economical and never longer. Opt-in per key; requires storing an encrypted copy of the prompt prefix (AES-256-GCM) because re-sending it is how the cache stays warm.
4. Auto-Tune — learns each key's real call rhythm (median gap between requests) and picks the cheapest cache settings, e.g. Anthropic's 5-minute vs 1-hour TTL, switching only when the math clearly favors it and showing the evidence.
5. Teams — organizations with shared workspaces, department/member CSV bulk import, org admin API tokens, budgets and audit logs.
6. Sub-tenants — one enterprise ck_ key serving many end-customers, each with its own cache policy, usage/savings attribution and warm slots (see the dedicated section below).

## Measured results (public benchmark)

10,000+ real, billed API calls; the same workloads run direct, hand-tuned, and through the proxy; all costs are the providers' own usage numbers at public list prices. Method, harness and raw logs are open source in the GitHub repo.

- Sparse support traffic (6–9 min idle gaps, claude-haiku-4.5): 67% cheaper than direct — net of all warming pings. Hand-tuning without warming was *more* expensive than doing nothing, because the cache expired in every gap while paying the write premium.
- 300-call classification batch with a shared prefix: 89% cheaper than SDK defaults.
- GPT-5.6 steady traffic: SDK defaults measured 0% prefix hits; through the proxy 97.8% hit rate (S6 cell, run-202607-v0100), up to 90% saved.
- Latency: time-to-first-token was equal or better through the proxy (a cache hit skips prompt prefill); the hop itself measured smaller than provider noise.

## Provider support matrix

- Anthropic: analytics + auto cache_control + breaker detection + Cache Warmer + 5m/1h Auto-Tune.
- OpenAI (incl. GPT-5.6+ and the Responses API): analytics + breaker warnings; on 5.6+ an explicit cache breakpoint and stable prompt_cache_key restore prefix caching. stream_options.include_usage is added when missing so streamed usage is still metered. /v1/completions and /v1/embeddings pass through with metering.
- Gemini: context-cache metering and savings pricing, unstable-prefix warnings.
- Grok (xAI): OpenAI wire format on the same endpoint; grok-* model names route automatically; a stable x-grok-conv-id cache-routing header is injected to lift hit rates (never overriding one you send).
- Where a provider already caches well on its own, traffic passes through at zero overhead — warming pings were measured there and turned off rather than billed.

## Sub-tenants (platforms & enterprises)

A platform serving many end-customers through one ck_ key tags each request with the customer it belongs to — no provisioning step; the headers alone work:

- X-Cache-Tenant: <id> — which end-customer the request belongs to (1–120 chars: letters, digits, . _ : -). Unlocks per-tenant policy resolution, per-tenant usage/savings attribution, and per-tenant warm slots.
- X-Cache-Warm-Slot: <id> — a warm slot inside the tenant, e.g. one per end-user. Each slot keeps that user's latest prefix warm; slots are pruned to the most recent N (default 16; per-tenant keepalive_max_slots, 1–128).
- X-Cache-Keepalive: on|off, X-Cache-Injection: on|off, X-Cache-Ttl: 5m|1h — per-request overrides. Precedence: request header > tenant policy > key setting.

Management API — authenticated with the ck_ key itself (x-api-key or Authorization: Bearer):

- GET /admin/v1/tenants — list tenant policy rows (?limit&after pagination).
- GET/PUT/DELETE /admin/v1/tenants/{tenant} — PUT is a partial upsert of {auto_cache_control, keepalive_enabled, keepalive_budget_usd_daily, anthropic_cache_ttl, keepalive_max_slots}; null clears a field back to inheriting the key's setting. DELETE offboards the tenant — drops its policy row and stops its warming.
- GET /admin/v1/tenants/{tenant}/stats?days=7 — requests, warming_pings, input/output tokens, cache read/write tokens, cost_usd, saved_usd.

Budgets stack: a tenant's keepalive_budget_usd_daily caps that tenant's warming pings, while the key-level daily budget still caps the whole key. Warming remains Anthropic-only. Enterprise gateways: GET/PUT/DELETE /admin/v1/gateway sets a per-key upstream gateway URL for Anthropic-wire traffic (operator-approved allowlist only); warming pings follow the gateway and replay the request's custom x-* headers so gateway-side routing and attribution keep working — contact support to have a gateway approved.

## Pricing

- Cloud: 20% of verified net savings (savings measured against list price, minus every warming ping spent on your behalf), charged after the month closes. Fees under $5/month are waived, never carried over. If it saves you nothing, you pay nothing. The dashboard shows the exact running fee all month.
- Self-host: free forever, Apache-2.0, one `docker compose up`. Cloud-only extras: zero ops, Auto-Tune, weekly reports and budget alerts.

## Security & privacy

- Prompt and response bodies are never stored by default — only token counts, model names, latency, status codes, and SHA-256 hashes of prefix blocks.
- You bring your own provider API keys; they are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, used only to forward your requests, and never logged.
- Per-account cache isolation; apps authenticate to the proxy with a Caching.ai key (ck_...).
- No lock-in: if the proxy is ever down, point the base URL back at your provider and you are running direct again.

## Integrations

Copy-paste recipes exist for Claude Code (officially supported via settings/env; plus a Cache Keeper plugin — `/plugin install cache@caching-ai` — that auto-warms the cache after every turn), Codex (native Responses API support), Cline/Roo, and any tool with a custom base-URL field. An agent-executable setup guide lives at https://caching.ai/agent-setup.md.

## FAQ (verbatim from the site)

Q: Do you store my prompts?
A: No. By default we store only token counts, model names, latency, status codes, and SHA-256 hashes of prefix blocks. The Cache Warmer is opt-in per key and stores an encrypted copy of your prompt prefix (AES-256-GCM) because re-sending it is how the cache stays warm — the trade-off is stated right on the toggle.

Q: How does the proxy authenticate?
A: You bring your own provider API keys. They're encrypted at rest, used only to forward your requests, and never logged. Your apps call us with a Caching.ai key instead.

Q: What's the latency overhead?
A: Streaming responses are piped through byte-for-byte with usage read on the fly — no buffering. Analytics writes happen after your response is already on its way.

Q: Which providers are supported?
A: All four — analytics and cache-breaker detection everywhere, with optimization where it measurably pays: auto cache_control and the Cache Warmer on Anthropic, and on GPT-5.6+ an explicit cache breakpoint plus a stable prompt_cache_key that restore the prefix caching the new models no longer do on their own (measured 0% → 97.8% prefix hits on steady traffic — S6 cell of our published benchmark). OpenAI, Gemini, and Grok hold their caches upstream — we measured warming pings there and turned them off instead of billing you for them.

Q: What does it cost?
A: Pricing is performance-based: 20% of what we verifiably save you, charged to your card after each month closes. Fees under $5 are waived. If we save you nothing, you pay nothing.

Q: My provider already caches automatically — why do I need this?
A: Right — the discount exists. The problem is how often you actually get it. Caches expire after ~5 idle minutes, and a single changed character at the start of your prompt silently breaks them. We keep the cache alive, catch what breaks it, and show you the hit rate you're really getting — most teams find it's far lower than they assumed.

Q: What is Auto-Tune?
A: It learns each key's real call rhythm — how far apart requests actually arrive — and picks the cheapest cache settings for it: the 5-minute vs 1-hour TTL on Anthropic. OpenAI, Gemini and Grok are managed automatically per model — nothing to configure. It only switches when the math clearly favors it, and shows you the evidence (median gap, sample size, projected savings) on the key.

Q: What happens if Caching.ai is down?
A: Your requests do pass through us, so an outage on our side would fail your calls — and the fix is the same one-line change you made when you connected: point the base URL back at your provider and you're running direct again. No lock-in, nothing to migrate.
